name: FERPA: The Records Belong to the Family
title: FERPA: The Records Belong to the Family
answer: FERPA gives families the right to see and control their children's education records, and schools generally need written consent before sharing personal information from those records. The school official exception allows sharing with outside companies only when the school controls how the data is used and kept, which is why pasting student information into a free chatbot is a privacy mistake. This matters because AI tools are common in classrooms while the law itself has not been updated for them.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: FERPA is the federal law that gives parents, and students once they turn 18, the right to inspect education records and decide who else may see them. As a general rule, a school cannot release personal information from those records without written permission. The school official exception is the part that matters most for AI because it permits a school to share records with an outside company doing work the school would otherwise do itself. The problem it solves is that schools need vendors, including AI vendors, to operate, but the exception only works when the school keeps direct control over the records through a contract. Without that control, a tool that seems helpful can become an unauthorized disclosure.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day school life, the exception is set up through the contract a district signs with a vendor, not through a teacher's judgment in the moment. A teacher who pastes a student's writing, grades, or behavior notes into a free chatbot has shared education records with a company the school has no agreement with, and that company is not under the school's direct control. The text does not give separate grade band examples, so the same rule applies wherever students are old enough to have education records. The habit to prevent is the casual paste into a tool nobody approved, and the text calls this the most common privacy mistake with AI in schools and the easiest to prevent. Schools make it work by routing AI use through approved tools covered by a data privacy agreement.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this idea with a legal and regulatory basis rather than an experimental one. It cites the U.S. Department of Education (2014) for the conditions attached to the school official exception, namely that the company must be under the school's direct control and may use records only for the authorized purpose. It also notes that FERPA's regulations were last updated in a major way in 2011, well before generative AI reached classrooms. The Education Department told Congress in 2024 that it planned a new rule to settle unresolved enforcement questions, and its 2026 agenda lists FERPA, but no proposed rule had been published as of the writing (Senate HELP Committee, 2024). Until that changes, the text says, schools are applying an old law to a new technology.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The exception is not open ended. A company receiving records must be under the school's direct control for using and keeping them, and it may use them only for the purpose the school authorized. It cannot sell the data or reuse it for its own products unless the school's agreement allows that. Direct control is established through the contract, which is why the data privacy agreement later in the chapter carries so much weight. The decisions that stay with people are the ones about which tools are approved, what the contract permits, and whether a given use of student information is authorized, and the text notes that until FERPA is updated, more of that weight falls on each district's own contracts and policies.
